catalog_quote: 6.2 There is already evidence to support the claim that tone functions lexically. In the last chapter, two distinctive tones, the low level and the high level were identified. These were assigned to syllable nuclei which were either single vowel sounds, or nasals. Monosyllabic word-types occurred with one of these two tones, and every possible sequence of the two tones occurred with disyllabic word-types: low-low, high-high, low-high, high-low. For word types with more than two syllables, it was shown that these could be broken down so that the different syllables of the word consisted of the various tone patterns already identified as occurring with monosyllabic and disyllabic word types. ... 6.4 Although we have recognised a contour tone, Kono is essentially a register tone language, because the dominant tonemic units are two level tones, a high and a low. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both halves of the deciding quotation are verbatim in the Manyeh 1983 PDF we hold text layer at the stated places (sec. 6.2 pdf p.172; sec. 6.4 pdf p.184 = printed 175). (2) The deciding source is a 310-pp phonology PhD (Leeds 1983) with its own instrumental chapter — the top-ranked descriptive work in Glottolog's list for kono1268 alongside Foday-Ngongu 1985; there is no reference grammar of this language. A Crossref search found Hogan & Manyeh 1996 (Phonetica), whose abstract independently characterises Kono as a two-level register tone language with downstep, consistent with the classification 'tonal'. Nothing seen suggests any author has proposed word stress or accent for Sierra Leone Kono. (3) list of works to obtain is short: Foday-Ngongu 1985 (not reachable online from here), Hogan & Manyeh 1996 (paywalled DOI), Lessau 1991 (print MA).
